intro.html: Some people say a great deal in a few words; others use a great many words to say very little. This topic gathers the words for both. Half praise economy (concise, succinct, pithy), a few describe people who simply talk very little (laconic, taciturn), and the rest describe a flood of talk (verbose, garrulous, voluble).

Few words, well chosen: concise, succinct, pithy, brevity. Few words, maybe too few: terse, laconic, taciturn. Many words: verbose (in speech or writing), garrulous (chatter about little things), voluble (fast, fluent, eager talk).

words.def: giving all the needed information in few words
words.ex: Her {concise} note said everything: “Pizza in the oven. Back at six.”
words.ctx: The first draft rambled on for ten pages, but the final report was {concise}: two pages that covered every key finding without a wasted word.
words.etym: From Latin concisus, “cut short,” from concidere: con (thoroughly) + caedere (to cut).

mn.text: Zoe’s report ran three pages, so she cut it to size: one tight paragraph that still says it all. Now it is {concise}.

scene.alt: A girl proudly holds up one short page, the long drafts in the trash, while a woman claps.

words.def: brief and clear; said in few words
words.ex: When the coach asked what went wrong, Lin gave a {succinct} answer: “We stopped passing.”
words.ctx: The museum’s labels are {succinct}: each one tells you what the object is, how old it is and why it matters, all in a single sentence.
words.etym: From Latin succinctus, “tucked up, belted,” as a traveler belts up a long robe to move quickly.
words.note: Say both c’s: suk-SINKT, like “success” at the start.

mn.cue: suk-SINKT: SINK it in one shot
mn.text: Kai sinks the ball in the bucket with one clean toss: no extra bounces, no wasted moves. A {succinct} answer is like that: it makes its point in one shot.

scene.alt: A boy cheers as his ball drops straight into a bucket in one clean toss.

words.def: brief, sometimes to the point of seeming rude
words.ex: The {terse} text, “K,” left Jamal wondering whether his sister was upset.
words.ctx: Grandma usually writes long, chatty letters, so her {terse} postcard, “Arrived. Raining. Love, G,” made the whole family laugh.
words.etym: From Latin tersus, “wiped clean, polished”: a terse sentence has every extra word wiped away.

mn.text: Chef Omar keeps his lips pursed while he cooks and answers every question with one word: “Busy.” “Later.” “No.” His answers are {terse}.

cast.say: What’s for dinner? Can I help? Is it…

scene.alt: A chatty boy asks a cook many questions; the cook answers with one word.

words.ex: The {laconic} rancher answered every question with “Yep” or “Nope.”
words.ctx: Though the reporters asked long questions about her record-breaking climb, the {laconic} mountaineer said only, “It was cold.”

roots.means: Laconia, the land around ancient Sparta

words.etym: From Greek Lakonikos, “of Laconia,” the region of ancient Sparta, whose speakers were known for short replies.

mn.text: Asked how his long, long trip across the desert went, the rancher says only, “Fine.” He lacks words to spare: he is {laconic}.

cast.say: So, how was the long trip across the whole desert?

scene.alt: A man asks a long question; the cowboy answers with a single word.

words.ex: Grandpa’s {pithy} advice fit on a sticky note: “Measure twice, cut once.”
words.ctx: The speech was long and dull, but its closing line was {pithy}: “Start small, start now.” People were still quoting it weeks later.
words.etym: From pith, the soft core of a plant stem; the pith of an idea is its core.

mn.cue: PIT-HY: a tiny PIT, a whole tree
mn.text: A tiny peach pit holds a whole tree inside it. A {pithy} saying is the same: a few words with a big idea packed in.

scene.alt: An old professor holds up a tiny fruit beside a big fruit tree: small seed, big tree.

words.def: shortness, especially in speech or writing
words.ex: The {brevity} of the speech delighted the hungry dinner guests.
words.ctx: Teachers praised her essay for its {brevity}: where others wrote ten pages, she made the same points clearly in three.
words.etym: From Latin brevitas, from brevis, “short,” the same root as brief and abbreviate.

mn.text: Nobody calls little Theodore by his whole name; he is just Theo. Brev- means brief, and {brevity} is the art of keeping it short.

scene.alt: A grandmother waves to a toddler; a sign shows the long name Theodore shortened to Theo.

words.def: using more words than are needed
words.ex: The {verbose} instructions took three pages to explain how to plug in a lamp.
words.ctx: His answer was so {verbose} that by the time he finally reached his point, half the class had forgotten the question.
words.etym: From Latin verbosus, “full of words,” from verbum, word.

mn.cue: VERB-HOSE: a fire hose of words
mn.text: Ask the lawyer a yes-or-no question, and words gush out like water from a fire hose: “Firstly, secondly, furthermore…” He is {verbose}.

scene.alt: A lawyer talks on and on as papers fly, and the judge falls asleep.

words.def: talking too much, especially about unimportant things
words.ex: Our {garrulous} seatmate told us about every one of her eleven cats.
words.ctx: The {garrulous} barber kept up a stream of chatter about the weather, his nephew’s soccer team and the price of eggs, hardly pausing to breathe.
words.etym: From Latin garrulus, “chattering,” from garrire, “to chatter.”

mn.text: Once Grandpa Gus starts talking, he runs on and on: the weather, his knees, the fish he almost caught. Gus is {garrulous}.

cast.say: And another thing! And then! And also…

scene.alt: A grandfather talks on and on while the boy listening falls asleep.

words.def: quiet by habit; saying very little
words.ex: Her {taciturn} uncle spoke perhaps ten words during the whole holiday dinner.
words.ctx: In class Dev was {taciturn}, rarely raising his hand or chatting, yet his notebooks were full of sharp ideas and funny drawings.
words.etym: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus, “silent,” the root of tacit.

mn.cue: TACIT TURN: his turn, and silence
mn.text: Around the campfire everyone takes a turn telling a story. When it is Omar’s turn, he just smiles and pokes the fire. He is {taciturn}.

scene.alt: At a campfire a woman says it is Omar’s turn to tell a story; he just sits quietly.

words.def: talking easily, quickly and at length
words.ex: The {voluble} tour guide chatted happily all the way up the mountain.
words.ctx: Shy in a big crowd, Rosa became {voluble} with close friends, talking fast and happily for hours about books, music and her plans.
words.etym: From Latin volubilis, “rolling, flowing,” from volvere, “to roll”: words roll easily off a voluble tongue.

mn.text: Lila and Maya talk like a volleyball game: words fly fast, bounce right back and never hit the ground. Both girls are {voluble}.

scene.alt: Two girls on the beach chatter fast while a ball flies between them.

after.cap: Brevity can be a gift or a chill; many words can be warm or wearing.

after.html: laconic and taciturn are close cousins. A laconic person answers, but very briefly (“Fine.”). A taciturn person tends not to talk at all and may seem unfriendly. And succinct is said suk-SINKT: both c’s count.

items.q: Uncle Ned sat through the whole family reunion saying almost nothing to anyone. Which word fits him best?
items.why: Taciturn describes someone who tends not to talk at all. Laconic fits someone who does answer, but in very few words.

items.q: Asked to describe her three-week trip, Ada said only, “Good trip.” Her reply was…
items.why: She answered, but in as few words as possible: that is laconic.

items.q: True or false: brevity is a noun meaning shortness.
items.why: True. Brevity (from Latin brevis, short) is the noun; brief is the adjective.

items.q: Which word carries the most criticism: talking too much about unimportant things?
items.why: Garrulous suggests tiresome chatter about little things. Voluble only says the talk is fast and fluent.

items.q: Type the word that means brief and clear; said in few words. It starts with s and has two c’s.
